clean: Environment block format (windows_policy.rs:31-34): the block is exactly `SystemRoot=<root>` followed by two zero UTF-16 units, so it ends in four zero bytes as CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT requires. A single variable needs no sorting. CREATE_FLAGS (windows_policy.rs:4) are SUSPENDED|EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT|NO_WINDOW|UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT.

Buffer lifetime: `environment` is a local Vec bound at windows_native.rs:661 and borrowed inside the closure run synchronously by create_and_release_attributes (windows_native.rs:701-714). It lives until spawn returns, and CreateProcessW copies the block. No resources are held when the call fails, because it runs before Job and pipe creation.

GetSystemWindowsDirectoryW contract (windows_native.rs:644-652): the buffer is 261 units with uSize equal to the buffer length. 0 means failure; a value >= 261 means too small, because the required size includes the null. The return value excludes the null, so `&buffer[..length]` is exact. Unpaired surrogates and a root-directory result such as `C:\` fail closed. The signature matches windows-sys 0.61.2 SystemInformation/mod.rs:30, and the Cargo feature was added to both dependency tables.

Validation and injection (windows_policy.rs:16-30): NUL, control characters, '=', reserved characters, dot and empty components, non-drive and UNC/verbatim forms, and over-260-unit roots are refused. There are no panicking slices: index 2 and 3 boundaries are guaranteed by the ASCII prefix check. The minimum-length 4→3 survivor is genuinely equivalent.

Inherit-nothing and no-credential property: lpEnvironment is non-null, so nothing is inherited. The single value comes from the OS API, never from std::env; windows_native.rs and windows_policy.rs have no env reads. It carries no secret, and the bootstrap secret still travels only over the private pipe. This matches POSIX env_clear (platform.rs:330).

Pre-READY adapter mechanics are evidence-backed by actual CI: in b74d867 the supervisor reported ChildExited. That error is reachable only after write_bootstrap_with_permit returned Ok (supervisor.rs:355-392). So CreateProcessW with HANDLE_LIST and JOB_LIST, the IsProcessInJob check, ResumeThread==1 and the bootstrap write all succeeded with the real frozen exe, and owned cleanup succeeded. The environment block is the only adapter launch input this diff changes.

Job limits: the owned Job sets only JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE (windows_native.rs:404), and the outer pipeline Job sets only 0x2000 (_native_package_process.py:950). There is no active-process limit (so conhost from CREATE_NO_WINDOW cannot hit one), no UI restriction and no breakaway dependence.

Stdio shape: the child pipe ends are opened synchronously (no FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED, windows_native.rs:298-311). stderr is an inheritable NUL handle (lines 670-680). The service sets O_BINARY and uses raw os.read/os.write (bootstrap.py:26-36,69-76; runner.py:47-67). Closing the parent end gives ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE, which the CRT reads as EOF, so the lease ends cleanly; the probe observed exit 0 on lease EOF. The non-frozen service launched with Rust std named-pipe stdio, Stdio::null stderr and SystemRoot passes on windows-2025 CI (python_runtime.rs:52-71; actual_python_service_accepts_native_proof_then_ready_version_health shows ok in the retained raw windows-2025 verify log in the scratchpad).

PATH, COMSPEC, PATHEXT, TEMP and locale at import and startup: the exact artifact reached READY with SystemRoot only (probe-observations.txt). The service source has no subprocess, tempfile, sqlite, home or environment reads (grep). The bootloader imports only USER32 and KERNEL32 (12-pe-service.stdout). The build is onedir (build-windows-runtime.py:333), so there is no extraction directory. Encoding does not matter for binary framing.

Reasoned, not observed: the payload locks (GENERIC_READ with FILE_SHARE_READ only, windows_native.rs:557-598) are compatible with LoadLibrary (read/execute access, shares read), with _wfopen and Python open (share read/write), and with stat calls that request attributes only. The supervisor-chosen port comes from an OS port-0 bind (platform.rs:117-124), so excluded port ranges are avoided.
No stale 'empty environment' claim remains in the specification, platform docs or code (git grep). The spec has no rule requiring an empty Windows environment.

Evidence packet integrity: all 20 retention-manifest entries match their bytes and SHA-256, with no unlisted files. The retained windows-15 actor stdout, stderr, result and upfront files equal the downloaded CI artifact apart from CRLF. The probe exe hash CA4D…CAC1 equals the pinned entrypoint_sha256.
There are 24 #[test] functions in windows_policy.rs, consistent with the recorded `24 passed`. I did not run them: the brief forbids builds or tests in this tree.

notes.title: Likely next Windows failure after READY: the actor checks listener release with an immediate bind of a port whose listener used SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE
notes.claim: Once the env fix lets the service reach READY, the Windows package actor runs code that has never executed on Windows. `assert_listener_released` (lines 12-15, called at line 246) does a single immediate `TcpListener::bind((LOCALHOST, port))` with no retry. The service's listener sets SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE (runner.py:156-158), and on shutdown uvicorn actively closes the client's keep-alive connection (the Rust client keeps one connection, client.rs:229-257). Microsoft's SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE guidance says that a connection accepted from an exclusive listener, left in TIME_WAIT after an active graceful close, can stop the port being re-bound until it expires. This comes from Windows documentation as I remember it; I did not check it against any file.
notes.failure_scenario: The hosted run on the next commit gets READY plus health, ready and version, and shutdown succeeds. Then `assert_listener_released(identity.bind_port)` gets AddrInUse and the test panics with "Owned listener must be released". That costs another hosted cycle, and someone could misread it as a supervisor cleanup defect.
notes.evidence: Supporting evidence from repository files: (a) the Unix branch of the same function avoids bind because "TIME_WAIT can outlive an exclusive listener" (package_validation.rs:18-19). (b) The retained Ubuntu actor stderr for this run records `server_active_close=1 ... legacy_bind=AddrInUse` (docs/evidence/m03-w07-ci-b74d867-terminal/ubuntu-15-package-actor.stderr line 3), so a bind oracle does fail after a server active close on Linux. (c) apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/api_client/tests/python_runtime.rs:160-162 notes that on Windows the former socket tuple "may remain unavailable briefly", even with no accepted connection, and uses a 1 s retry budget. The Windows branch (package_validation.rs:12-15) has none. It is not verified on Windows. Any change to the oracle must keep proving that the listener was released, not loosen it.

notes.title: Windows 11 desktop behaviour with a SystemRoot-only block is unproven beyond the Server 2025 probe
notes.claim: All of the following is speculation, not observed. The probe proves SystemRoot is enough on the windows-2025 runner image. On desktops, three launch conditions could still stop the service before READY. (1) A third-party Winsock LSP or namespace provider whose catalog DLL path uses a variable other than %SystemRoot% (such as %windir% or %ProgramFiles%) could not be expanded, giving the same WinError 10106. (2) Smart App Control or antivirus could block the unsigned PyInstaller exe or its pyds. (3) Defender's first-scan latency over the onedir tree counts against the 10 s startup budget (supervisor.rs:50), which also covers runtime verification and hashing. Windows' own environment blocks carry `windir` next to `SystemRoot`. Adding `windir` with the same OS-reported value would be a design choice, not a correction.
notes.failure_scenario: On a Windows 11 desktop with such a provider or policy, the service exits or times out before READY. The supervisor reports ChildExited or StartupTimeout, and the child's stderr goes to NUL.
notes.evidence: Speculative. Nothing in the repository or the CI artifacts shows any of these on the runner. The exe imports only USER32 and KERNEL32 (b74d867-win/art/pipeline/12-pe-service.stdout). The service binds and loops back only on numeric 127.0.0.1, so no hostname lookups through namespace providers are needed. The Windows 11 VM campaign is the planned proof.

notes.title: KI-0143 rationale is partly inaccurate about %SYSTEMROOT%\Temp for standard users
notes.claim: KI-0143 says a standard non-elevated Windows 11 user cannot write to "those directories". That holds for the Windows directory, which is where GetTempPathW falls back. But the default ACL on C:\Windows\Temp, as I know it, grants BUILTIN\Users create-file and create-folder rights (CI)(S,WD,AD,X), with CREATOR OWNER full control. If so, Python's tempfile fallback would probably succeed for a standard user, writing into a machine-wide directory. That is a placement and privacy problem, not the CI-pass/desktop-fail split the KI describes. This is from Windows knowledge and was not checked on a host.
notes.failure_scenario: A future fix shaped by the KI's wording would test only for write failure. It would miss the fact that tempfile output lands, apparently successfully, in a shared machine directory.
notes.evidence: KNOWN_ISSUES.md:72 text. The CPython 3.12 tempfile and ntpath.expanduser behaviour the KI describes is otherwise accurate: with no USERPROFILE or HOMEPATH, `~\AppData\Local\Temp` stays relative and is skipped, and the next candidate is %SYSTEMROOT%\Temp.

verified.title: CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT (0x400) now matters, but the only test of it compares the constant with itself
verified.claim: The change turns the environment block from [0,0] into a non-empty UTF-16 block. That makes the 0x0000_0400 (CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT) bit of CREATE_FLAGS load-bearing. The only test of the flags, creation_requires_atomic_job_assignment_suspension_and_no_console, asserts launch_plan(..).flags == CREATE_FLAGS, which is true whatever the constant holds, and checks only that 0x10, 0x8 and 0x01000000 are absent. No test requires 0x400 to be present.
verified.failure_scenario: Mutate line 4 to drop `| 0x0000_0400`. Every non-Windows test and the Windows verify job still pass, because the comparison is tautological and service_environment is unaffected. On Windows, CreateProcessW would then read the UTF-16 block 'S\0y\0s\0...' as an ANSI block (per the documented CreateProcessW contract; not checked against a file). The child would get junk single-letter entries and no SystemRoot, so the WinError 10106 / ChildExited failure (KI-0142) would come back. Only the hosted Windows package actor (step 15) would catch it. Before this change the bit was not load-bearing: an all-zero 4-byte block is empty as either ANSI or Unicode.

votes.why:
I could not refute this finding. Every factual claim matches the working tree.

1. **The constant.** windows_policy.rs:4 is `pub const CREATE_FLAGS: u32 = 0x0000_0004 | 0x0008_0000 | 0x0800_0000 | 0x0000_0400;`.

2. **The only flags test is tautological.** It is `creation_requires_atomic_job_assignment_suspension_and_no_console`, around lines 244-251. It asserts `launch_plan("C:\\runtime\\a.exe").unwrap().flags == CREATE_FLAGS`. `launch_plan` sets `flags: CREATE_FLAGS` at line 85, so this holds for any value of the constant. The test's only check on the value is negative: `CREATE_FLAGS & (0x10 | 0x8 | 0x01000000) == 0`. Nothing requires 0x400 to be set. Despite its name, it also never checks 0x4 (suspended) or 0x80000 (extended startup info), which was already true before this change.

3. **No other test in the repo checks the bit.** `git grep` for CREATE_FLAGS, 0x0000_0400 and CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT (excluding docs/evidence) returns only windows_policy.rs lines 4, 85, 248 and 250. Other hits on 0x400 elsewhere are unrelated: windows_policy.rs:385/395 test the reparse-point file attribute, and the Python scripts test `st_file_attributes & 0x400`. scripts/_native_package_process.py:1024 passes its own `0x4 | 0x80000 | 0x400` to a separate Python CreateProcessW harness. That does not test the Rust constant. platform_adapters/policy.rs only calls `launch_plan` for a path check.

4. **The bit now matters.** The diff removes `LaunchPlan.environment: [0, 0]`. windows_native.rs:661 builds `service_environment(&system_windows_directory()?)`, and lines 708-709 pass `plan.flags` with `environment.as_ptr().cast()`. The block is now non-empty UTF-16 ("SystemRoot=...\0\0"), so whether CreateProcessW reads it as Unicode depends on 0x400. The old block was 4 zero bytes, which is empty read either way.

5. **The failure scenario is plausible, but I did not check it against a file.** This part rests on the documented CreateProcessW contract and the kernelbase behavior I know. Without CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT the block is treated as ANSI and scanned for a double-NUL byte. For UTF-16LE ASCII text that splits into one-letter entries with no '='. CPython on Windows skips environment entries that have no '=', so SystemRoot would be missing. The probe recorded for this change shows that leads to WinError 10106 when importing asyncio.

**Why not BLOCKING.** The mutation would not reach a release undetected. The hosted Windows package actor runs the real frozen service through `windows_native::spawn`: scripts/package_validation.rs, the test `service::package_validation::packaged_runtime_health_auth_and_owned_cleanup`, wired in from scripts/native_package_pipeline.py:908-929. It is the check that already failed with ChildExited in this exact way. So the gap is a missing unit-level assertion, not a regression with no guard at all.

**Why still a real defect.** The constant now carries correctness, and the project counts surviving mutants against a test (see the memory notes). A one-line positive assertion, such as `assert_eq!(CREATE_FLAGS & (0x4 | 0x80000 | 0x400), 0x4 | 0x80000 | 0x400)`, would kill the mutant on every platform.

I could not refute this finding. I checked it against the working tree using read-only commands only.

1. The constant is unchanged by the diff. windows_policy.rs:4 still reads `CREATE_FLAGS: u32 = 0x0000_0004 | 0x0008_0000 | 0x0800_0000 | 0x0000_0400`.
2. The only test that touches the flags is creation_requires_atomic_job_assignment_suspension_and_no_console (lines 245-251). It checks two things:
   - `launch_plan("C:\runtime\a.exe").unwrap().flags == CREATE_FLAGS`, which only proves that launch_plan uses the constant. It says nothing about what the constant contains.
   - `CREATE_FLAGS & (0x10|0x8|0x01000000) == 0`, which only checks that those bits are absent.
   Nothing requires 0x400 to be set. The same is true of 0x4 and 0x80000, even though the test name says it "requires" them; that gap was already there before this change.
3. A repo-wide grep over tracked files for CREATE_FLAGS, 0x0000_0400 and CREATE_UNICODE finds nothing else. The other hits are unrelated: mod.rs, the launch_plan call in platform_adapters/policy.rs, and the 0x400 file-attribute checks in the Python scripts.
4. windows_native.rs has no unit tests. The only real Windows spawn that would catch the bug is packaged_runtime_health_auth_and_owned_cleanup in scripts/package_validation.rs. The package pipeline injects it as a cfg(test) module (native_package_pipeline.py:908-929), so it runs only in the hosted pipeline's package-actor step. The ordinary verify suites do not run it.
5. The docs do not claim the flag is pinned. KNOWN_ISSUES KI-0142 and TEST_EVIDENCE list 23 mutants, all against service_environment, and none of them drops 0x400.

The diff does make the bit matter. The environment changes from `[0u16,0]`, which is four zero bytes and so an empty block whether read as ANSI or Unicode, to a UTF-16 block reading `SystemRoot=...\0\0`.

Not checked against a file (based on how I understand CreateProcessW works): without CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT, CreateProcessW treats lpEnvironment as ANSI and stops at the first pair of zero bytes. The block would then read as single-letter entries ('S', 'y', ...) with no SystemRoot, which reproduces the WinError 10106 / ChildExited failure. Python's subprocess and Rust's std::process both set 0x400 whenever they pass an environment, for the same reason.

Why NON_BLOCKING and not BLOCKING: the current code is correct, because 0x400 is present. The gap is only that a future regression would be caught late, by the hosted Windows package actor. KI-0142 closure already requires fresh hosted package results, so the regression would not go unnoticed. Adding `assert_ne!(CREATE_FLAGS & 0x400, 0)`, and the same for 0x4 and 0x80000, costs little. It also fits the project's mutation-testing practice, because a mutant that drops 0x400 currently survives every test outside the hosted package actor.

verified.title: The accepting side of service_environment is barely pinned: a stricter minimum length or an uppercase-only drive check survives
verified.claim: The positive test uses only 'C:\\Windows' (10 bytes) and 'D:\\OS Root Ω\\Windows'. The mutation campaign tried only the downward change of the minimum length (4→3, which is equivalent). It never tried the upward changes, which are not equivalent and survive. KI-0142 and TEST_EVIDENCE say the tests pin 'each refusal rule'. That holds for the refusal direction, but what the function accepts is not pinned.
verified.failure_scenario: I ran a scratch copy of service_environment (rustc in the scratchpad, not in the repo) against both committed tests, reproduced verbatim. Mutants `bytes.len() < 5` through `< 10` pass both tests but refuse valid roots such as 'C:\\W' or 'X:\\WINNT'. Replacing is_ascii_alphabetic with is_ascii_uppercase also passes but refuses 'c:\\Windows', which the original accepts. Each regression fails closed: the service would never start (SpawnFailed). Hosted CI would not catch the length mutants either, because the runner root is 'C:\\Windows' (10 bytes).

votes.why:
I could not refute the finding. I checked it against the real code with my own probe instead of trusting the reviewer's copy, which is not verbatim. That copy is /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tanishkalwad-jobapplyv2/17ee071f-b2d5-4e6f-a57e-209b35ae06c1/scratchpad/se-probe/m2.rs, and it rewrites the tests as a hand-made `tests_pass` helper.

**How I checked.** I copied lines 16-35 (`service_environment`) and lines 178-228 (both new tests) of /Users/tanishkalwad/jobapplyv2/apps/desktop/src-tauri/src/service/windows_policy.rs byte for byte into /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tanishkalwad-jobapplyv2/17ee071f-b2d5-4e6f-a57e-209b35ae06c1/scratchpad/skeptic1-probe/base.rs. The only addition was a stub `SupervisorError` enum. I made each mutant with sed and ran it with `rustc --test` inside the scratchpad. Nothing ran in the repo.

**Results:**
- The original passes (2 passed).
- Raising the minimum length from 4 to 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 or 10 lets every test pass (2 passed).
- Raising it to 11 is caught (1 failed), because "C:\\Windows" is exactly 10 bytes.
- Changing `is_ascii_alphabetic` to `is_ascii_uppercase` lets every test pass.
- Changing it to `is_ascii_lowercase` is caught, and so is removing the length check (it panics on "").

So the accepting side really is unpinned. The function's stated contract would accept roots like "C:\\W", "X:\\WINNT" or "c:\\Windows". Stricter mutants refuse them and no test notices. The campaign record /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tanishkalwad-jobapplyv2/17ee071f-b2d5-4e6f-a57e-209b35ae06c1/scratchpad/mutants-ki0142.txt confirms that only the downward 4→3 change was tried.

Hosted CI would not catch the length mutants either. The retained docs/evidence/m03-w07-ci-b74d867-terminal/diagnostic/probe-observations.txt shows the runner's SystemRoot is C:\Windows, which is 10 bytes.

**One inaccuracy in the finding.** The phrase "each refusal rule" appears only in KI-0142 (docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md). TEST_EVIDENCE lists the mutants it ran and states the 22/23 result accurately. Its claim that the 4→3 survivor is equivalent is true. No recorded evidence is false. Only KI-0142's "pin each refusal rule" goes too far: the threshold of the minimum-length rule is not pinned.

**Why NON_BLOCKING and not higher.** Every surviving mutant fails closed: the spawn fails, nothing is injected and no safety boundary is weakened. They also do not change behaviour for any realistic root. From general Windows knowledge, which I did not check against a file, Windows 10/11 and Server always report "<uppercase drive>:\\Windows" from GetSystemWindowsDirectoryW. The one observed hosted value matches that.

**Why not NOT_A_DEFECT.** The contract described in KI-0142 and in the doc comment is defined only by what the function refuses. Valid inputs at the lower edge and lowercase drives are part of that contract, and a regression there would leave the service unable to start. The suggested fix is cheap: add a short lowercase-drive positive case such as "c:\\W" to `service_environment_is_exactly_the_os_windows_directory`, or narrow KI-0142's wording.

I could not refute this. I checked it against the files and with my own probe.

1. The code matches the finding. In the working tree, windows_policy.rs:16-35 refuses when `bytes.len() < 4` or `!bytes[0].is_ascii_alphabetic()`, among other rules. The only positive test (lines 178-186) uses exactly "C:\\Windows" (10 bytes) and "D:\\OS Root Ω\\Windows" (21 bytes). The refusal test's only positive cases are the 260-unit `longest` string and its 261-unit refusal.

2. My own reproduction. I wrote a new probe, separate from the reviewer's m2.rs: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tanishkalwad-jobapplyv2/17ee071f-b2d5-4e6f-a57e-209b35ae06c1/scratchpad/skeptic2-se/p.rs. I compiled it with rustc in the scratchpad, not in the repo. It copies the function verbatim and both committed tests as assertions. Results:
- The original passes.
- The minimum-length mutants 3 through 10 all pass the tests. 11 and 12 fail.
- An uppercase-only drive check (`is_ascii_uppercase`) passes the tests.
- The original accepts "C:\\W", "c:\\Windows" and "C:\\WINNT". The surviving mutants refuse at least one of them, so mutants 5 through 10 and the uppercase one are not equivalent. Only 4→3 is equivalent.

3. The mutation log is in scratchpad/mutants-ki0142.txt. Its 23-mutant set tried only `min length 4 -> 3` for the lower bound and no drive-case narrowing. That matches the finding.

4. The docs are not false. TEST_EVIDENCE says the 23 listed mutants kill 22 and the survivor is equivalent, which is true for that set. It names the boundary as 260/261 UTF-16 units. KI-0142's "each refusal rule" holds in the refusal direction. KI-0142's "the exact length boundary" is ambiguous: a reader could take it to include the minimum, and the minimum is not pinned. Together with "the survivor is equivalent", the docs make the campaign sound more complete on the accepting side than it is.

Why NON_BLOCKING:
- The current code is correct, and nothing here is a security or trust-boundary problem. Every surviving mutant fails closed: the service would not start, with SpawnFailed.
- The practical exposure is small. From general Windows knowledge, not checked against any file: on supported Windows 10/11, GetSystemWindowsDirectoryW almost always returns "C:\\Windows". Lowercase-drive or very short Windows directories are unusual.
- Still, it is a real hole in the tests. A later refactor could raise the minimum to anything up to 10, or narrow the drive check to uppercase, and pass both unit tests. The hosted runner, whose root is "C:\\Windows", would not catch the length mutants either.
- This matches how the earlier reviewer's refusal-side test gaps were classified and fixed.

The fix is trivial: add a short lowercase-drive positive case such as "c:\\W" to service_environment_is_exactly_the_os_windows_directory. Optionally, narrow KI-0142's "exact length boundary" wording to the 260/261 upper bound.

verified.title: KI-0143 says a standard user cannot write %SYSTEMROOT%\Temp, which is likely wrong
verified.claim: KI-0143 says tempfile falls back to %SYSTEMROOT%\Temp and GetTempPathW falls back to the Windows directory. It then says the elevated CI runner can write "those directories" but a standard non-elevated Windows 11 user cannot, so a feature that writes temporary files could pass CI and fail on desktops.
verified.failure_scenario: From Windows documentation knowledge, not checked against any retained file: the default ACL on C:\Windows\Temp gives BUILTIN\Users (CI)(S,WD,AD,X), and CREATOR OWNER gets full control of what it creates. A standard user can therefore create and delete their own files there, so Python's tempfile would most likely work on a desktop. The real issue for tempfile is a shared, machine-wide location visible to administrators, not a failure. The GetTempPathW fallback to C:\Windows\ is not writable by standard users, so that half of the claim is right. As worded, the KI predicts the wrong failure mode for Python temp files.

votes.why:
I could not refute this finding. The KI's fallback chain is correct, but its writability claim is wrong for the directory Python tempfile actually picks.

**Checked against files**
- **Service Python version.** The service runtime is pinned to CPython 3.12.13 (scripts/build-windows-runtime.py:281).
- **tempfile candidate order.** I read /Users/tanishkalwad/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.12.13-macos-aarch64-none/lib/python3.12/tempfile.py. `_candidate_tempdir_list` tries, in order:
  1. TMPDIR, TEMP and TMP.
  2. `expanduser(r'~\AppData\Local\Temp')`.
  3. `expandvars(r'%SYSTEMROOT%\Temp')`.
  4. c:\temp and the other fixed paths.
  5. The current directory.
- **The home path stays relative.** In ntpath.py of the same build, `expanduser` returns the path unchanged when USERPROFILE and HOMEPATH are both unset.
- **That relative path is resolved against the working directory.** `_get_default_tempdir` turns it into an absolute path under the service's working directory (plan.directory in windows_native.rs). That folder normally does not exist, so the open fails with FileNotFoundError, which is an OSError, and the loop moves on.
- **Result for tempfile.** With an environment of SystemRoot only (service_environment, passed to CreateProcessW at windows_native.rs:661/702), tempfile probes C:\Windows\Temp. The probe opens a file with `os.open` (O_CREAT|O_EXCL), writes to it, and unlinks it. That probe, not a general "can write" test, is what decides whether the directory is used.

**Not checked against any file (Windows documentation knowledge)**
- **Default ACL of C:\Windows\Temp.** It gives BUILTIN\Users:(CI)(S,WD,AD,X) and CREATOR OWNER:(OI)(CI)(IO)(F). So a standard, medium-integrity user can create files and subfolders there and gets full control, including DELETE, over what they create. tempfile's probe would therefore succeed and return C:\Windows\Temp on a standard-user Windows 11 desktop.
- **Supporting evidence for that ACL.** C:\Windows\Temp is a well-known shared folder that standard users can write to. Planting files there is an established local privilege-escalation technique. That is why newer Windows sends SYSTEM processes to C:\Windows\SystemTemp via GetTempPath2.
- **GetTempPathW fallback.** It falls back from TMP to TEMP to USERPROFILE to the Windows directory. Standard users cannot create files directly in C:\Windows, so that half of the KI's sentence is right.

**Conclusion**
KI-0143 (docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md line 61) says a standard non-elevated user "cannot" write "those directories", and that wording includes %SYSTEMROOT%\Temp. That is most likely wrong. For Python tempfile, the realistic desktop outcome is a silent success in a machine-wide folder that SYSTEM and Administrators can read, not a failure. That matters for privacy, given the rule that resume and application content must never land in shared or persistent locations. Only the native GetTempPathW case (for example SQLite) fails as the KI predicts. The KI does mark itself "not reproduced; source review", but it states this ACL claim as fact. PROJECT_STATUS.md and TEST_EVIDENCE.md describe KI-0143 only as a "temp/home fallback risk" and do not repeat the wrong claim.

**Severity: NON_BLOCKING**
- The KI correctly records a latent LOW/OPEN risk with nothing exercised today.
- Its resolution (explicit private temp and data directories, tested as a standard user) is still correct and would also cover the real privacy failure mode.
- The KI-0142 code fix is unaffected.
- It is still more than a NOTE: the record predicts the wrong failure mode, a loud failure instead of a silent privacy exposure. A future implementer could expect CI-versus-desktop breakage that never happens and miss that temporary files land in a shared folder.
- Fix: one sentence. Separate tempfile's shared, admin-readable C:\Windows\Temp from GetTempPathW's unwritable C:\Windows.

I could not refute this finding. It is a real problem, but a small one.

**What the files show**
- docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md:61 (KI-0143) names two fallbacks:
  - Python's tempfile falls back to %SYSTEMROOT%\Temp.
  - GetTempPathW falls back to the Windows directory.
- It then says the elevated CI account "can write those directories; a standard non-elevated Windows 11 user cannot, so a later feature that writes temporary files could pass CI and fail on desktops." The KI presents this as fact; no retained file tests it.
- No file tests whether those directories are writable:
  - Neither the evidence packet (docs/evidence/m03-w07-ci-b74d867-terminal/) nor the b74d867-win artifacts mention Windows\Temp, icacls or tempfile.
  - TEST_EVIDENCE.md:12445 only says the risk was "recorded as KI-0143".
  - The KI itself says "Reproduction: not reproduced; source review".
- windows_policy.rs::service_environment emits only `SystemRoot=<GetSystemWindowsDirectoryW>`, so the KI's premise that SystemRoot is the only variable is accurate.
- windows_native.rs calls CreateProcessW with the parent token: I found no restricted token, AppContainer, integrity-level change or CreateProcessAsUser. A standard user's service therefore runs at medium integrity with that user's normal rights.
- A grep of services/orchestrator/src found no tempfile, sqlite, expanduser, os.environ or getenv use. That confirms the KI's "nothing fails today".

**From Windows and CPython documentation (not checked against any file)**
- The default ACL on C:\Windows\Temp gives:
  - BUILTIN\Users: (CI)(S,WD,AD,X), meaning they can add files and subfolders but not list the folder.
  - CREATOR OWNER: (OI)(CI)(IO)(F).
- CPython 3.12's `_get_default_tempdir` picks a directory by creating, writing and deleting a probe file there. In this environment:
  - `~\AppData\Local\Temp` stays relative and becomes `<cwd>\~\...`. That path does not exist, so the check skips it.
  - `%SYSTEMROOT%\Temp` expands through the SystemRoot variable to C:\Windows\Temp. The probe file succeeds there because the user can add files and owns, with full control, the file it creates.
- So a standard user's tempfile calls would most likely succeed in C:\Windows\Temp rather than fail. The risk is a shared, machine-wide location that administrators and SYSTEM can read, which is what the KI title ("machine-wide locations") already describes.
- The GetTempPathW half is right. Its fallback order is TMP, TEMP, USERPROFILE, then the Windows directory, and C:\Windows is read/execute only for Users. Native callers such as SQLite temp files would fail for a standard user.

**Why NON_BLOCKING**
- It is a factual error in a LOW, OPEN KI that already says it was not reproduced.
- It does not change today's behavior: the service writes no temporary files.
- The planned fix (explicit private temp/data directories, tested as a standard user) and the KI title stay correct.
- The fix is a wording change: separate the two directories, so tempfile reads as a privacy/hygiene risk and native GetTempPathW callers read as a desktop failure.
- It is not merely a NOTE, because the project contract asks that recorded claims be ones that were actually observed, and this sentence states an untested, likely wrong prediction as fact in a canonical file.
- Caveat: hardened enterprise images may tighten C:\Windows\Temp; I am describing the stock Windows 11 default ACL.

findings.title: SystemRoot-only may not cover third-party Winsock providers on end-user machines (reasoned, not checked)
findings.claim: The fix rests on the default Winsock catalog expanding only %SystemRoot%. Reasoned from Win32 knowledge and not checked against any file: a third-party layered or namespace provider registered with another variable, such as %ProgramFiles% or %windir%, would still fail to load. Sockets of that protocol would then fail with WSAEPROVIDERFAILEDINIT (10106) under the SystemRoot-only block.
findings.failure_scenario: On a user's Windows 11 machine with such a provider installed, the frozen service fails on `import asyncio` before READY, exactly as in KI-0142. The supervisor reports only ChildExited, because stderr goes to NUL and no exit code is recorded. Hosted windows-2025 runners and the planned disposable Windows 11 VM are clean images, so neither can expose this.
findings.evidence: Not observed. The probe (probe-observations.txt) shows READY with SystemRoot only on a clean runner image. KI-0142 already notes that the child's stderr goes to NUL and ChildExited carries no exit code, so a recurrence would be undiagnosable from the supervisor record.
